---
title: "Quiz: image-to-image translation and hallucination"
---

Short questions on paired and unpaired translation and on generated detail. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** A U-Net trained with squared error to predict a nuclear stain from transmitted light gives sharp nuclei but a faint haze where a cytoplasmic marker should be. Why the haze?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the squared error converge to when the input does not decide the target?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The marker is not visible in the input, so for a given input the target varies (spots here or there, or none). The squared error is minimised by the average of those targets: a haze. The nuclei are visible, so their average is sharp.
:::

---

**Q2.** What does the discriminator of a conditional GAN (pix2pix) receive, and why not just the output image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A realistic stain of a different cell would fool a discriminator that sees only the output.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The pair (input, output). It must judge whether the output is a realistic stain **for this input**, so the generator cannot ignore its input.
:::

---

**Q3.** For an ambiguous pixel, which has the smaller expected squared error against the truth: the conditional mean, or a sample from the conditional distribution? By what factor?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A sample is an independent draw from the same distribution as the truth.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The mean. A sample has twice the mean squared error ($2\operatorname{Var}$ against $\operatorname{Var}$), i.e. $\sqrt 2$ times the RMSE. The sample looks real; the mean is accurate on average but looks like no real cell.
:::

---

**Q4.** A cycle-consistent translator from label-free to stained images reaches zero cycle loss and fools both discriminators. Does that prove the stained output of each cell is its true stain?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which pairs did it see?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. It saw no pairs. It matches the two distributions and can be undone, which many different maps achieve (in 1D both an increasing and a decreasing map). Which output belongs to which input is not constrained.
:::

---

**Q5.** A virtual-staining network was trained on untreated cells, in which 20 % show a marker. You apply it to treated cells; the generated images show the marker in 25 % of cells. What can you conclude about the treatment?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the network do where the input does not show the marker?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Nothing. Where the marker is not visible in the input, the network paints what was typical in training, about 20 %. The real share could be 80 %. Measure on real stains of treated cells, or validate the translator on treated cells with ground truth.
:::

---

**Q6.** You run a translator with 16 different noise inputs on the same image. In one region the 16 outputs agree, in another they differ strongly. What does each tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where does the input decide the output?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Agreement: the input determines the output there (or the model is overconfident; only ground truth tells). Disagreement: the input does not decide the output; any single output there is a guess. Disagreement flags hallucination risk; agreement does not prove correctness.
:::
